en: To make someone feel isolated, unwelcome, or unfriendly
hook: ALIEN-ATE: makes you feel like an ALIEN.
story: Rafi's constant bragging about his scores alienated his study group. One by one, his friends stopped inviting him, until he was studying alone. To alienate is to make someone feel isolated or turn them against you. Harsh policies can alienate voters.

en: Lack of interest, enthusiasm, or concern
hook: A-PATHY: without (a) feeling (pathos).
story: Only twelve percent of students voted in the union election. The candidates blamed apathy: nobody seemed to care who won. Apathy is the absence of interest or emotion. The opposite of love isn't hate; it's apathy, total indifference.

en: Appropriate to the situation; with reference to
hook: APROPOS: APPROPRIATE to the PURPOSE.
story: At the graduation ceremony, the speaker told a story about a fisherman who never gave up. It was perfectly apropos for students facing an uncertain future. Apropos means fitting and relevant. 'Apropos of the exam,' meaning 'regarding the exam,' introduces a related topic.

en: Appropriate or suitable; having a tendency; quick to learn
hook: APT: APpropriaTe. Also, APTitude for learning.
story: Calling Dhaka 'the city that never sleeps' is apt; traffic honks even at three in the morning. Mitu is an apt student who learns quickly, but she's apt to forget things when tired. Apt means suitable, or likely to do something, or quick to learn.

en: A loose outer garment; something that hides (noun); to conceal (verb)
hook: CLOAK: like an invisibility cloak, hiding the truth.
story: The meeting was cloaked in secrecy: no phones, no notes, no names. Under the cloak of charity, the organization was actually laundering money. A cloak is a loose cape; figuratively, it's anything that hides the truth. To cloak is to conceal.

en: General agreement among a group
hook: CONSENSUS: everyone gives their CONSENT.
story: After two hours of debate, the family reached a consensus: the trip would be to Cox's Bazar, not Sylhet. Everyone agreed in the end. Consensus means general agreement. Scientific consensus on climate change is overwhelming.

en: To twist out of shape; to give a misleading account of
hook: DIS-TORT: TWISTED (torque) out of shape.
story: The funhouse mirror distorted Arif's reflection, making him look tall and thin. The newspaper distorted the minister's words too, quoting half a sentence to make it sound outrageous. To distort is to twist shape or meaning. Distorted facts can be worse than lies.

en: Moving apart in different directions; differing
hook: DI-VERGE: two paths going different ways.
story: The two brothers grew up in the same house but chose divergent paths: one became a monk, the other a stockbroker. Divergent means moving apart or differing. Divergent opinions are views that don't agree. Its opposite is convergent.

en: Ecstatically happy
hook: ELATED: ELEVATED with joy.
story: When Nadia opened the email and saw 'Congratulations! Full scholarship,' she was elated. She screamed, hugged her mother, and called every relative. Elated means extremely happy and excited. It's the opposite of crestfallen.

en: To fill with delight; to charm
hook: EN-CHANT: like a magical CHANT that casts a spell.
story: The old storyteller enchanted the village children with tales of tigers, kings, and flying horses. They sat silent, eyes wide, for hours. To enchant is to delight or charm deeply, as if by magic. An enchanting smile captures every heart.

en: Firmly established and difficult to change
hook: EN-TRENCHED: dug deep into a TRENCH, impossible to move.
story: The habit of giving dowry was so entrenched in the village that, even after laws banned it, families still practiced it quietly. Entrenched means firmly fixed, like a soldier dug into a trench. Entrenched beliefs, entrenched interests, entrenched corruption.

en: Originating from a distant foreign country; strikingly unusual
hook: EXOTIC: EXternal, from the outside world.
story: At the international food fair, Sara tried exotic dishes: Ethiopian injera, Peruvian ceviche, and Korean kimchi. To the visitors from abroad, her mother's panta bhat seemed exotic too. Exotic means foreign and strikingly unusual.

en: Taking unfair advantage of people or resources for selfish benefit
hook: EXPLOITATIVE: EXPLOITS people.
story: The factory paid workers two dollars a day for fourteen hours of work, with no breaks and no safety gear. Activists called it exploitative. Exploitative means using people or resources unfairly for profit. Child labor is a clear example of an exploitative practice.

en: Able to be predicted or expected
hook: FORE-SEE-able: can be SEEN BEFORE it happens.
story: Building houses on the riverbank without any protection was a foreseeable disaster; everyone knew the river would flood. For the foreseeable future, Tanvir will be studying every evening. Foreseeable means predictable. In the foreseeable future means as far ahead as we can predict.

en: To abandon or give up entirely
hook: FOR-SAKE: abandon FOR your own SAKE.
story: When the business failed, his so-called friends forsook him; nobody returned his calls. Only his old school friend stood by him. To forsake is to abandon someone, especially when they need help. He also forsook his bad habits after that difficult year.

en: To give pleasure or satisfaction to
hook: GRATIFY: makes you GRATEFUL and happy.
story: Seeing his former student become a successful doctor deeply gratified the old teacher. All those years of hard work had paid off. To gratify is to please or satisfy. Instant gratification is the pleasure of getting what you want immediately, like scrolling instead of studying.

en: To pay careful attention to (advice or warning)
hook: HEED: use your HEAD and listen.
story: The fishermen who heeded the cyclone warning returned to shore safely. Those who ignored it were caught in the storm. To heed is to pay attention to advice or a warning. Heedless means careless, not paying attention.

en: Having or showing good judgment
hook: JUDICIOUS: like a wise JUDGE.
story: Mitu made a judicious use of her limited time: weak areas first, timed practice tests on weekends, and enough sleep every night. Judicious means wise and sensible. A judicious decision is carefully reasoned. Synonyms: prudent, sagacious.

en: Expressed clearly; easy to understand; mentally clear
hook: LUCID: full of LIGHT (lux), crystal clear.
story: The teacher's explanation of compound interest was so lucid that even Rafi, who hated math, understood it on the first try. Lucid means clear and easy to understand. A patient having a lucid moment is thinking clearly. Synonyms: pellucid, limpid.

en: Directly relevant to the matter at hand
hook: PERTINENT: PERTAINS to the topic.
story: At the interview, Arif kept his answers pertinent: no stories about his childhood, only examples directly related to the job. The panel was impressed. Pertinent means relevant. Impertinent originally meant irrelevant, and now means rude.

en: Conformity to accepted standards of behavior or morals
hook: PROPRIETY: PROPER behavior.
story: In the old days, rules of propriety meant young men and women couldn't meet without an elder present. Today, propriety still demands that you don't answer phone calls during a funeral. Propriety means correctness of behavior, a synonym of decorum.

en: Sparkling; brilliantly lively and clever
hook: SCINTILLATING: sparkles like a tiny spark (scintilla).
story: The debate champion delivered a scintillating speech, full of sharp wit, clever examples, and perfect timing. The audience laughed, gasped, and finally stood up to applaud. Scintillating means brilliantly lively and witty, sparkling like light.

en: Causing great excitement; presented in a shocking way to attract attention
hook: SENSATIONAL: designed to excite the SENSES.
story: 'Celebrity's Secret Life Revealed!' screamed the sensational headline. The article itself said almost nothing. Sensational means causing excitement, often through exaggeration. Sensational journalism prefers shock over truth. Informally, it can also mean wonderful.

en: Highly developed and complex; having refined, worldly taste
hook: SOPHISTICATED: from SOPHIA, wisdom; refined and advanced.
story: The new phone uses sophisticated software that recognizes your face in the dark. Its designer is a sophisticated woman who has lived in Paris and collects modern art. Sophisticated means complex and advanced, or worldly and refined.

en: Angry or bitter disagreement; conflict
hook: STRIFE: STRIKES and FIGHTS.
story: Years of political strife left the country exhausted: strikes, protests, and clashes in the streets. Inside Tanvir's family, inheritance strife split brothers apart. Strife means bitter conflict. Civil strife is conflict within a nation.

en: Presented in a subtle, restrained, and effective way
hook: UNDER-STATED: stated less loudly than it could be.
story: Among guests in flashy outfits, Nadia wore a simple white sari with a thin silver border. Her understated elegance drew more compliments than anyone's gold. Understated means subtle and restrained, not showy. It's the opposite of ostentatious.

en: Having no moral principles; dishonest
hook: UN-SCRUPULOUS: has no SCRUPLES (conscience).
story: The unscrupulous travel agent took money from fifty families, promising jobs in Malaysia, then disappeared. Unscrupulous means without moral principles, willing to cheat. The opposite is scrupulous, careful to do what's right.

en: Truthfulness; accuracy
hook: VERACITY: VERy accurate. 'Vera' means true.
story: Journalists questioned the veracity of the minister's claim that unemployment had fallen by half; no data supported it. Veracity means truthfulness or accuracy. Don't confuse it with voracity, which means a huge appetite.

en: Extremely harmful or poisonous; bitterly hostile
hook: VIRULENT: like a VIRUS, spreading poison.
story: The new strain of flu was virulent, spreading fast and causing severe illness. Online, the debate about it turned virulent too, full of insults and hatred. Virulent means highly harmful, or intensely hostile. Virulent criticism is bitter and poisonous.

en: Liable to change rapidly and unpredictably, especially for the worse
hook: VOLATILE: like a VOLCANO, could explode any moment.
story: The stock market was volatile: up five percent on Monday, down seven on Tuesday. Rafi's uncle has a volatile temper too; one wrong word and he explodes. Volatile means unstable and unpredictable. In chemistry, volatile liquids evaporate quickly.
